section: Fundamental Rights - Article 12 (State), Article 13 and doctrines of eclipse, severability, waiver
subsections: Article 12 - meaning of State, other authorities, instrumentality cases

accepted.s:
Which of the following is included within the expression ‘State’ under Article 12 of the Constitution of India?
1. The Government and Parliament of India
2. The Government and Legislature of each State
3. All local authorities
4. Other authorities in India or under the control of the Government of India
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
accepted.x: Article 12 includes the Union Government and Parliament, State Governments and Legislatures, local authorities, and other authorities in India or under the control of the Government of India.
accepted.tq: Use complete constitutional enumeration and check whether any category has been omitted.
accepted.sec: Article 12 - meaning of State, other authorities, instrumentality cases

accepted.s: Which one of the following cases laid down the tests for determining whether a body is an instrumentality or agency of the State?
o: R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority
accepted.x: R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority (1979) laid down the tests for identifying an instrumentality or agency of the State.
accepted.tq: Match the case with its distinctive constitutional holding rather than its year alone.
accepted.sec: Article 12 - meaning of State, other authorities, instrumentality cases

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the decision in Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib:
1. A society running a Regional Engineering College was treated as ‘State’.
2. The constitutional test depends on how the body was created and controlled, not merely on its legal form.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
accepted.x: In Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib (1981), the society running a Regional Engineering College was held to be ‘State’. The Court emphasised creation and control rather than the formal legal form of the body.
accepted.tq: Separate the substance of governmental control from the formal label of an institution.
accepted.sec: Article 12 - meaning of State, other authorities, instrumentality cases

accepted.s: In which of the following cases was it held that a body may be regarded as ‘State’ when it is financially, functionally and administratively dominated by the Government?
o: R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority
accepted.x: Pradeep Kumar Biswas (2002) held that financial, functional and administrative domination by the Government is a significant basis for treating a body as ‘State’.
accepted.tq: Use the three-part domination test as the identifying phrase for the correct case.
accepted.sec: Article 12 - meaning of State, other authorities, instrumentality cases

accepted.s: Which one of the following was the principal holding in Rajasthan SEB v. Mohan Lal (1967)?
o: Private bodies are always subject to writ jurisdiction
A society running a Regional Engineering College is not a public authority
Only bodies incorporated directly by Parliament can be ‘State’
Statutory bodies are included within ‘other authorities’
accepted.x: Rajasthan SEB v. Mohan Lal (1967) recognised statutory bodies as ‘other authorities’ for the purposes of Article 12.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the statutory-body principle from the later instrumentality tests.
accepted.sec: Article 12 - meaning of State, other authorities, instrumentality cases

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. A body’s formal legal form is by itself decisive in determining whether it is ‘State’ under Article 12.
2. Government share capital may be relevant in applying instrumentality or agency tests.
3. Deep and pervasive governmental control may be relevant in determining whether a body is ‘State’.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
accepted.x: Statements 2 and 3 are correct because government share capital and deep and pervasive control are relevant factors. Statement 1 is false because Ajay Hasia held that creation and control, rather than form alone, are material.
accepted.tq: Spot the absolute formulation that wrongly makes legal form conclusive.
accepted.sec: Article 12 - meaning of State, other authorities, instrumentality cases

accepted.s: Which of the following is NOT ordinarily correct regarding writ petitions against private bodies?
o: The ordinary rule is subject to the circumstance of State collusion
Writs ordinarily lie against every private body because Article 12 includes all institutions
A writ may become maintainable where the State acts in collusion with a private body
Writs do not ordinarily lie against private bodies
accepted.x: Writs do not ordinarily lie against private bodies merely because they perform an activity. An exception may arise where the State acts in collusion with the private body.
accepted.tq: Reject the option that uses an overbroad ‘every’ formulation and ignores the ordinary rule.
accepted.sec: Article 12 - meaning of State, other authorities, instrumentality cases

accepted.s: A private organisation performs a public activity, but no governmental authority is shown to be involved in the alleged violation. Which position is most consistent with the general rule concerning writs?
o: A writ can never lie against a private organisation under any circumstances
A writ ordinarily lies because every public activity makes the organisation ‘State’
A writ does not ordinarily lie merely because the organisation performs a public activity
A writ lies only when Parliament specifically authorises the organisation
accepted.x: Writs do not ordinarily lie against private bodies merely on the basis of their public activity. The rule is not absolute, since State collusion can alter the position.
accepted.tq: Apply the ordinary rule while avoiding the absolute trap in the words ‘every’ and ‘never’.
accepted.sec: Article 12 - meaning of State, other authorities, instrumentality cases

accepted.s: The demand to make the right to vote a Fundamental Right concerns a right which is presently regarded as:
o: A legal right derived exclusively from Article 21
A statutory right under Section 62 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, with a constitutional basis under Article 326
A constitutional right enforceable only under Article 32
accepted.x: The right to vote is presently treated as statutory under Section 62 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, and is constitutionally connected with Article 326. It is not presently a Fundamental Right.
accepted.tq: Separate a statutory electoral right from a Fundamental Right and identify both cited provisions.

accepted.s: The Supreme Court has reaffirmed that the rights to vote and contest elections are:
o: Natural rights outside the constitutional framework
Fundamental Rights available under Part III
accepted.x: The rights to vote and contest elections have been reaffirmed as statutory rights, rather than Fundamental Rights under Part III.
accepted.tq: Discriminate between the related but distinct rights to vote and contest and their legal status.

accepted.s: Which one of the following groups of provisions is commonly described as the ‘golden triangle’ of the Constitution?
accepted.x: Articles 14, 19 and 21 are collectively described as the golden triangle because of their interrelationship in protecting liberty and individual rights.
accepted.tq: Recall the standard constitutional grouping rather than selecting adjacent Fundamental Rights articles.

accepted.s:
Which of the following statements regarding Fundamental Rights is correct?
1. They operate as a check on governmental power.
2. They protect minorities.
3. They limit Parliament through Article 13.
4. They are regarded as a bulwark of liberty and the rule of law.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
accepted.x: Fundamental Rights check governmental power, protect minorities, support liberty and the rule of law, and limit Parliament through Article 13.
accepted.tq: Test several connected constitutional purposes and choose the complete combination.

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the constitutional position in Britain from that in India regarding Fundamental Rights?
o: Britain has no codified Fundamental Rights; its rights rest on conventions and the rule of law
India, unlike Britain, protects rights only through conventions
Britain has a single written code of Fundamental Rights identical to Part III of India
Britain has no protection of rights because it follows neither conventions nor the rule of law
accepted.x: Britain does not have codified Fundamental Rights in the Indian constitutional sense; protection rests largely on conventions and the rule of law.
accepted.tq: Compare the source and form of rights protection instead of confusing absence of codification with absence of rights.

accepted.s:
Which of the following Articles and provisions were inserted by the First Amendment Act, 1951?
1. Article 31A
2. Article 31B
3. The Ninth Schedule
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
accepted.x: The First Amendment Act, 1951 added Articles 31A and 31B and introduced the Ninth Schedule. The amendment is associated with the constitutional protection of certain land reform laws.
accepted.tq: Treat the amendment, its two Articles and the Schedule as one connected constitutional package.

accepted.s: With reference to the Ninth Schedule, which statement is correct?
o: All laws placed in it are permanently immune from every form of judicial review
It contains only provisions relating to elections
Its protective effect has been subjected to limitations by the decision in I.R. Coelho (2007)
It was created by the Forty-Fourth Amendment Act, 1978
accepted.x: I.R. Coelho (2007) limited the absolute character of Ninth Schedule protection by permitting judicial scrutiny where basic-structure principles are affected.
accepted.tq: Use the later judicial limitation to reject the extreme claim of complete and permanent immunity.

accepted.s:
Arrange the following developments in chronological order:
A. Decision in Rajasthan SEB v. Mohan Lal
B. Decision in R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority
C. Decision in Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib
D. Decision in Pradeep Kumar Biswas
accepted.x: The cases were decided in 1967, 1979, 1981 and 2002 respectively: Rajasthan SEB, R.D. Shetty, Ajay Hasia and Pradeep Kumar Biswas.
accepted.tq: Fix the earliest and latest cases first, then place the two closely related instrumentality decisions.
accepted.sec: Article 12 - meaning of State, other authorities, instrumentality cases
